source: Medaka / Liquidworld authors (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
finding: A prompt that forces recursive goal decomposition plus per-step state tracking beats plain chain of thought on a liquid-mixing planning test, mostly for strong models.
numbers: Pass@1 total: Claude Sonnet 4.6 CoT 77.8 -> Medaka 94.5; Gemini 3 Flash 65.6 -> 82.0; GPT-5.4 74.3 -> 78.5 (tie with AoT+); GPT-4o 25.7 -> 36.9; Llama 3.3 70B 26.6 -> 40.6; Gemma4 4B 55.7 -> 61.0; Gemma4 2B 26.3 -> 30.5. 3 rollouts per problem, 7 models.
limits: Thinking mode turned off for all models. One synthetic domain. Preprint. Medaka uses 1.8 to 3.8 times the tokens of CoT (median).
agent_relevance: Goal decomposition as a prompt gives a real gain at about 2-4x tokens, but it must be paid for against best-of-3.

source: Medaka / Liquidworld authors (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
finding: Gains concentrate where difficulty is structural: nonlinear, coupled and multi-goal problems. Weak models do not gain on nonlinear problems.
numbers: Nonlinear pass@1 CoT / AoT+ / Medaka: Claude 33.3 / 55.3 / 87.4; Gemini 16.4 / 21.4 / 50.9; GPT-5.4 28.9 / 49.1 / 46.5 (Medaka below AoT+). Multi-goal Claude 50.4 -> 89.5. Distractor vessels Claude 73.8 -> 94.0, GPT-4o 10.7 -> 42.9. Nonlinear Gemma4 4B 14.5 -> 12.6, Gemma4 2B 10.1 -> 11.9, Llama 15.1 -> 15.1.
limits: Medaka does not always beat the rival: on GPT-5.4 nonlinear it is worse than AoT+. Small open models show no gain on nonlinear problems; authors say they lack the capability.
agent_relevance: The scaffold unlocks latent skill; it does not create skill. Expect no gain when the model cannot do the sub-step. Gate by capability.

source: Medaka / Liquidworld authors (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
finding: Test-time compute check: Medaka pass@1 beats the CoT best-of-3 oracle on 4 of 7 models.
numbers: Claude: CoT pass@3 86.8 vs Medaka pass@1 94.5. Gemini: CoT pass@3 67.2 vs Medaka 82.0. Not true for GPT-5.4 and both Gemma4 models.
limits: Oracle best-of-3 favours CoT, so the comparison is conservative. Token ratio 1.8-3.8x.
agent_relevance: This is the equal-token test our G7 asks for. Run the same oracle best-of-k control for every scaffold element.

source: Medaka / Liquidworld authors (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
finding: Ablation: removing either the recursive-goal module or the state-tracking module lowers accuracy.
numbers: Claude 94.5 full; minus state tracking 90.5 (-4.0); minus recursive module 91.0 (-3.5). Gemini 82.0 full; minus recursive 76.0 (-6.0); minus state tracking 75.1 (-6.9). 3 trials per problem.
limits: Only two models ablated. Effects are 3.5 to 6.9 points, so decomposition alone is a modest part; state tracking matters as much. Module effects need not add.
agent_relevance: Goal decomposition and exact state tracking should be separate, separately tested pieces in S6/O5.

source: Medaka / Liquidworld authors (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
finding: Failure modes of search-style prompts: guess-and-patch of continuous values, state drift, locally correct but globally inconsistent arithmetic.
numbers: Example: model reaches 2 L target volume but composition (20,25,55)% instead of (13.43,30.52,56.05)%; another empties a vessel then reuses it.
limits: Qualitative, from inspected failures of GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B on linear problems.
agent_relevance: Greedy difference reduction on one component at a time fails when components are coupled. Detect coupling and solve globally in code.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Re-analysis argues the reported collapse on Tower of Hanoi is partly output-length and format limits, not failed reasoning. Asking for a program that prints the solution restored high accuracy at 15 disks.
numbers: Hanoi needs 2^N-1 moves. At 10 tokens per move, max N is about 12-13 for a 64k output limit. Collapse was reported before N=9, well below that limit. Models tested with a Lua-function prompt at N=15: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5, under 5,000 tokens.
limits: Author states results are preliminary with no statistical power (budget). Co-written with an LLM. A comment, not a controlled replication; an earlier draft had a token-limit error that was corrected.
agent_relevance: Do not make the model enumerate long move lists. Have it emit the recursive procedure and run it in code (G2, program does the stepping).

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Claims the River Crossing set includes unsolvable instances, so zero scores there are not reasoning failures.
numbers: Says Missionaries-Cannibals with boat capacity 3 has no solution for N>5 (N>=6 in the original test).
limits: The original paper page we read says N>=6 was dropped and mentions capacity k=4, so the comment's capacity may not match the original. Unresolved from our reading.
agent_relevance: Verify solvability before scoring planning benchmarks; a solver check belongs in the harness.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Argues Hanoi has a trivial one-rule decision per move, so move count is a poor measure of planning difficulty; Blocks World needs real search.
numbers: Hanoi branching factor 1 given the recursion; Blocks World branching O(N^2); optimal Blocks World plans NP-hard, near-optimal plans linear time.
limits: Argument only, no new data on Blocks World.
agent_relevance: Measure difficulty by search branching, not solution length, when picking tasks for the agent.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Reasoning models show a complexity wall on puzzle planning. Giving the exact recursive algorithm in the prompt did not move the wall.
numbers: Hanoi: near perfect at N=5 (31 moves), moderate N=5-7, near zero at N>=8. First error around move 40 for N=8 and about move 100 for N=10. Checker Jumping collapse around N=4 (24 moves). Algorithm in prompt: collapse at about the same N. Blocks World, DeepSeek-R1 at temperature 0 collapses at N=4; with sampling at N=30.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the HTML, not the PDF, first 100,000 of 145,000 characters. Lawsen disputes token-limit and solvability design. Failing to execute a known algorithm fits an execution-reliability reading and also a length-limit reading.
agent_relevance: Knowing the means-ends procedure is not enough. The program must execute it, as in our design where code decides transitions.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Reasoning effort first rises with difficulty, then falls near the collapse point though token budget remains.
numbers: Thinking tokens drop at the threshold, most in o3-mini variants, less in Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking. 64k max generation.
limits: Summary read; no exact curve values taken.
agent_relevance: A stopping rule keyed to model effort would miss this; the adaptive-stopping subfield should test it.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: Backward Chaining for Automated Reasoning in Natural Language
finding: Backward chaining (start from the goal, decompose to subgoals, cache results) beats forward chaining and CoT on deep proofs.
numbers: Depth-5 relative gain: ProofWriter-PUD +44% vs CoT and +56% vs Selection-Inference; PrOntoQA +37% vs CoT and +113% vs SI; ParaRules +43% vs CoT (as stated in the text).
limits: Label accuracy; gains grow with proof depth. It is a 4-module few-shot design on a large LM, not a single prompt.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that goal-first decomposition helps on deep reasoning chains; use where chains are long and the goal is checkable.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: Backward Chaining for Automated Reasoning in Natural Language
finding: Proof accuracy shows CoT often reaches the right label with a wrong proof.
numbers: On ProofWriter depth 5, CoT produced correct chains for only 28% of examples; hallucination was the main error source (48%). LAMBADA mostly produced correct chains.
limits: Suggests spurious shortcuts in ProofWriter-PD. Label accuracy overstates reasoning.
agent_relevance: Grade the chain, not only the answer (G3). A right label from a wrong chain is not a pass.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: Backward Chaining for Automated Reasoning in Natural Language
finding: Forward chaining degrades as the search space grows; a backward goal keeps the search narrow.
numbers: Selection-Inference success per step falls at later inferences on PrOntoQA depth 5. Of cases where a proof existed but SI said UNKNOWN: only 29% had no redundant inferences; 7% repeated the same fact all 5 times; 10% had only 2 unique inferences.
limits: Forward vs backward CoT alone gave comparable label accuracy; forward CoT was better on PUD. The gain comes from the modular design, not direction alone.
agent_relevance: Direction is not magic. Credit the decomposition plus caching, and test direction separately.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2025) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
finding: Step-by-step planning prompts help only when they match the problem class, and the help fades as problem size grows past the examples.
numbers: Table-to-stack Blocksworld, 261 instances. GPT-4 zero-shot 3.83%; stacking-specific CoT 59.3%; universal algorithm CoT 51.3%; progression proof CoT 6.89%; domain n-shot 6.13%. GPT-4-Turbo: zero-shot 19.1%, stacking prompt 40.6%, universal 37.1%. Claude-3-Opus: zero-shot 9.96%, stacking 24.5%, universal 37.1%.
limits: Two to three models, one domain family plus three synthetic domains. A classical solver (Fast Downward) scores 100% on all instances tested.
agent_relevance: A procedure shown in the prompt does not become a general algorithm. Put the procedure in code, keep the model for slot-filling.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2025) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
finding: Self-consistency lowered accuracy on these prompts, and CoT gains do not generalise to longer stacks.
numbers: Paper text: self-consistency performance dropped (appendix table 3). In synthetic tasks, CoinFlip stays above 90% until 31 steps; LastLetterConcatenation and arithmetic fall back to direct-prompt accuracy as steps grow, while only surface properties (Levenshtein distance) stay improved.
limits: Exact self-consistency deltas not taken; only the paper's statement and partial table rows were read.
agent_relevance: Votes on a wrong shared procedure do not fix it (G4).

source: Sel et al. (2025) Algorithm of Thoughts+ (AoT+), ICLR 2025
finding: A single-prompt search trace with periodic restating of the current state (memoization) cuts state hallucination and, per the authors, reaches or beats LLM-Modulo with an external verifier on Blocksworld and Logistics.
numbers: Human baseline 78% on Blocksworld; vanilla GPT-4 about 30%, and 14% on Logistics (cited from Valmeekam 2023). Tokens with GPT-4, Blocksworld total: AoT+ 2,067.8, LLM-Modulo 6,452.9, CoT 650.7; Logistics AoT+ 5,606.1 vs LLM-Modulo 23,015.3. Attention on solution steps in Llama-2-13B: AoT 86.3% vs AoT+ 27.0% (Blocksworld).
limits: Per-model accuracy table was not extracted; the paper says AoT+ passes the 78% human level with GPT-4 or Claude. Self-Refine gave only marginal gains over CoT.
agent_relevance: Restating state every few steps is cheap and works. Our code can do it exactly instead of asking the model.

source: Sel et al. (2025) Algorithm of Thoughts+ (AoT+), ICLR 2025
finding: Random search trajectories worked as well as human-intuition trajectories in the in-context search examples.
numbers: AoT+R vs AoT: Game of 24 70.0 vs 71.0; Crossword 54.0 vs 52.0; Creative Writing 7.59 vs 7.58 (ToT 69.0, 46.5, 7.56; CoT-SC 9.0, 15.6, 6.93).
limits: Applies to prompt examples, not to real planners.
agent_relevance: The form of search, not the cleverness of the example order, carries the gain. Avoid costly hand-built heuristic tables.

source: Sel et al. (2025) Algorithm of Thoughts+ (AoT+), ICLR 2025
finding: State error rate: memoization reduces state hallucination with search depth.
numbers: 200 Logistics games, solution depth 20, 20 states sampled per depth, Llama 3.1 70B: AoT+ shows lower state error than AoT (values only in a figure).
limits: Figure values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Count state errors with code; this metric is cheap to add to our harness.

source: Spitz, Minsky, Bessellieu (1984) Subgoal length versus full solution length in predicting Tower of Hanoi performance
finding: With total solution length held constant, the number of steps to the first subgoal predicted difficulty. A longer first subgoal meant lower scores.
numbers: Two groups of 20: third and fourth grade children and retarded young adults (mean IQ 60, mean MA 9.58). Mean scores Shorter vs Longer Subgoal set: children 7.2 vs 5.4 (t(19)=5.38, p<.001); retarded 5.0 vs 3.4 (t(19)=3.06, p<.01). Group F(1,36)=22.95, problems F(5,180)=15.23. 18 trials each.
limits: Small special samples, 3-disk problems only. Planning time before the first move was unrelated to performance, unexpectedly. Link to adult MEA is inferred.
agent_relevance: Difficulty tracks look-ahead depth to the next subgoal. Cap the look-ahead for one operator application and re-plan.

source: Clement & Richard (1997) Knowledge of domain effects in problem representation: the case of Tower of Hanoi isomorphs
finding: Isomorphs with identical problem spaces differ in difficulty because the context steers which viewpoint on the action is chosen. Planning cannot start until the right viewpoint is chosen.
numbers: Experiment 1: 60 college students, 15 per condition, 4 isomorphs (move vs change operator; transformation vs change-of-state viewpoint). Moves: viewpoint effect F(1,56)=7.48, p=.008; change-of-state versions needed about half as many moves. Time: viewpoint F(1,56)=12.097, p=.001; transformation versions took twice as long. Interaction on time F(1,56)=7.193, p=.009.
limits: Experiment 2 (60 more subjects, 15 per cell) did not show a memory-load account; differences there were not significant. Bayes-fiducial effect sizes, not standard d. Rival account: processing load (Kotovsky and Fallside, 1989).
agent_relevance: Difficulty can sit in the representation, before any means-ends step. Reframe before searching, triggered by an impasse signal (G1).

source: Clement & Richard (1997) Knowledge of domain effects in problem representation: the case of Tower of Hanoi isomorphs
finding: Argues the Hanoi rules must first be turned into prerequisites for suboperators (leaving a state, entering a state) before the global means-ends heuristic can be used.
numbers: Qualitative argument built on Experiments 1-2. Adults who plan well on Hanoi fall back on child-like trial and error on hard isomorphs.
limits: Not tested as a separate manipulation.
agent_relevance: MEA needs a correct operator model first. Add an operator-precondition check step before choosing operators.

source: Fansher, Shah, Helie (2022) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: External (computer) presentation raised completion but mental presentation gave shorter solutions. Solving mentally first pushed people toward goal-recursion-like strategies on the second problem.
numbers: Experiment 1: 138 recruited, final n=129, 4-disk and 5-disk. Completion 100% computer vs 91% mental (chi2(1)=4.45, p=.03). 5-disk completion 93% computer vs 63% mental (B=-2.67, p=.001). Experiment 2: 572 Prolific workers; 5-disk completion 87.37% vs 55.25%. Self-reported use of move-sequence memory and subgoals higher mentally (F(1,112)=33.86 and 4.46); trial and error higher on computer (F(1,112)=5.51, p=.02).
limits: Strategy reports are self-reported 0-100% sliders, not behavior. 15-minute limit. Goal recursion measured only by proxy.
agent_relevance: Written-out external state speeds progress but invites trial and error; an internal plan step first gives tighter solutions. Plan first, then execute from tracked state.

source: Fum & Del Missier (2001) Adaptive selection of problem solving strategies (CogSci)
finding: Strategy choice on 4-disk Hanoi shifted with instructions: accuracy emphasis fit the perceptual strategy; effort emphasis fit Karat's limited look-ahead strategy. Selective-search and goal-memory models fit poorly.
numbers: 34 undergraduates, 8 trials, df 29 in ANOVAs (instruction effect on errors F(1,29)=6.57, p<.05; on time F(1,29)=7.83, p<.01). ACT-R simulation: perceptual strategy within the 99% CI on 100% of trials in the accuracy group (MAD 2.899); Karat strategy 87.5% in the effort group (MAD 2.264). Optimal solutions rare: 12% (accuracy) and 5% (effort).
limits: Small N, one simulation study. Only errors fitted, not times. Fit does not prove the strategy was used.
agent_relevance: Instructions and effort cost choose the strategy; our scaffold should pick strategy by cost, not use one fixed method.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Sussman anomaly
finding: Classical limit of MEA-style planners: when goals are treated as independent, solving one subgoal undoes another.
numbers: Problem: B on table, C on A, A on table; goal A on B on C. Noninterleaved planners must undo a finished subgoal either way. Later planners interleave subgoals. Sussman's thesis published 1975.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, no performance data.
agent_relevance: Order subgoals by dependency and allow undoing. Check for goal interference before committing a subgoal.

source: Problem solving as probabilistic inference with subgoaling (2016) PLOS Computational Biology
finding: A model with subgoal priors explains human Hanoi effects: preference for paths staying inside a community, graded time cost at bottlenecks, and failure on counterintuitive moves. Perceptual subgoal priors (not look-ahead) produce the human errors.
numbers: 3-disk, 27-state graph, 39 transitions. Preferred path reached 72% after four resampling iterations, matching human data. Counterintuitive move S27 to S20: optimal 7 moves; most frequent perceptual solution 9 moves; means of 25 runs. Lesion model used 85% perceptual and 15% algorithmic particles.
limits: Human sample sizes not in the text I read; lesion data come from earlier studies with a five-disk version. Only 100,000 of 141,000 characters read, via fetch summary. The paper contrasts its model with backward, impasse-driven subgoaling in the literature.
agent_relevance: Good subgoal choice, not search depth, separates performers. Score subgoal quality and test a perceptual-versus-look-ahead rule.

source: MAKER (2025) Solving a million-step LLM task with zero errors
finding: Extreme decomposition into single-step microagents with per-step voting is claimed to run over one million LLM steps with zero errors; prior LLM runs derailed after a few hundred steps.
numbers: Abstract only: over 1,000,000 steps, zero errors.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, so model, vote size and cost are unchecked. It relies on voting, which G4 says is not independent for single-answer problems; Hanoi steps are deterministic so errors can be caught by rule.
agent_relevance: If true, per-step verification beats clever planning on long procedures. Use code checks per step rather than model votes.

source: Greeno (1974) Hobbits and orcs: acquisition of a sequential concept; Thomas (1974) An analysis of behavior in the hobbits-orcs problem
finding: From a search snippet only: subjects solved hobbits-orcs until two error-free solutions. Greeno argued the organization is forward in the problem, in contrast to GPS's retroactive organization. Thomas concluded subjects plan in small subsequences of moves, not single moves.
numbers: No numbers: full text was blocked (403).
limits: Not opened. OpenAlex citation counts: Thomas 99, Greeno 105. A 1980 Perceptual and Motor Skills paper (author unseen) reported no compelling evidence that people need look-ahead on this problem.
agent_relevance: MEA describes poorly the detour step where the solver moves away from the goal. The detour must be allowed by rule.

source: Jeffries, Polson, Razran, Atwood (1977) A process model for missionaries-cannibals and other river-crossing problems
finding: Cited as a process model of river-crossing problems; details not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only the citation was seen (via a search snippet). Treat as an unverified pointer for the A-angle document.
agent_relevance: Same boundary: the backward move is where difference reduction breaks.
